section.title: React vs Angular vs Next.js vs TypeScript
section.subtitle: UI libraries, a full framework, a React meta-framework and the typed language — how each builds modern frontends.

topics.title: What It Actually Is
topics.learn: Library vs framework vs language — they solve different layers of the problem.

react.definition: React is a UI library for building component trees with JSX. It handles rendering and state; you choose router, state manager and build tools yourself.

angular.definition: Angular is a full-featured framework (by Google) with components, DI, routing, forms and HTTP built in — everything is provided out of the box.

next.definition: Next.js is a React framework adding SSR/SSG, file-based routing, API routes and image optimisation — production React without config.

ts.definition: TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JS. It's not a framework — it adds static types used by React, Angular and Next.js.

topics.title: Components
topics.learn: The building blocks of each UI approach.

react.definition: Components are functions returning JSX. Props flow down; state lives inside with useState/useReducer. Composition over inheritance.

angular.definition: Components combine a TypeScript class, an HTML template and CSS in one unit, wired with decorators and dependency injection.

next.definition: Next.js uses React components — Server Components by default (render on server, zero JS shipped) and Client Components ('use client') when interactivity is needed.

ts.definition: TypeScript models components as typed interfaces/classes — props, state and component contracts become compile-time checked.

topics.title: State Management
topics.learn: Where component data lives and how it updates.

react.definition: Local state via useState/useReducer; shared state lifted up or externalised with Context, Redux, Zustand or TanStack Query.

angular.definition: Components hold state as class properties; services (singletons via DI) share state app-wide. RxJS Observables drive reactive state.

next.definition: Next.js splits state: server data fetched in Server Components or via React Server Actions; client UI state still uses React hooks / Context / external stores.

ts.definition: TypeScript types your state shape — discriminated unions model status (idle/loading/error), generics type stores and hooks.

react.definition: React has no built-in router — React Router is the standard: declarative <Route> components, nested routes, loaders and navigation hooks.
react.code:
import { Routes, Route, Link } from 'react-router-dom';

<Routes>
  <Route path="/" element={<Home/>} />
  <Route path="/users/:id" element={<User/>} />
</Routes>

<Link to="/users/1">Profile</Link>

angular.definition: Angular ships @angular/router — route configs with lazy loading, guards, resolvers and child routes configured in TypeScript.

next.definition: Next.js uses file-system routing: folders under app/ become routes, dynamic segments use [param], and layouts nest automatically.
next.code:
app/
├── page.tsx          → /
├── users/
│   ├── page.tsx      → /users
│   └── [id]/
│       └── page.tsx  → /users/:id
└── layout.tsx       → wraps all pages

ts.definition: TypeScript types route params and search params — Next.js generates typed helpers; React Router/Angular params get explicit types.

topics.title: Data Fetching
topics.learn: Getting server data into the UI.

react.definition: React fetches via useEffect + fetch/axios, or libraries like TanStack Query (caching, retries, loading states) — all client-side after mount.

angular.definition: Angular's HttpClient returns Observables; the async pipe in templates subscribes automatically, and interceptors add auth headers globally.

next.definition: Next.js fetches on the server: async Server Components await data directly (cached by default), plus revalidation strategies and Route Handlers for APIs.

ts.definition: TypeScript types the API boundary — response shapes become interfaces, fetch wrappers return typed Promises, generics parameterise queries.

react.definition: React is styling-agnostic: CSS modules, styled-components, Tailwind, or plain CSS — you pick. CSS-in-JS libs colocate styles with components.

angular.definition: Angular components have encapsulated styles by default (scoped per component), plus global styles, Sass support and Angular Material components.

next.definition: Next.js supports all CSS options plus built-in CSS Modules, Sass, Tailwind and styled-jsx — styles are optimised and scoped automatically.

ts.definition: TypeScript doesn't style anything itself — but typed CSS-in-JS libs (styled-components, vanilla-extract) give type-safe style props and tokens.

topics.title: TypeScript in Each
topics.learn: How each ecosystem uses (or doesn't use) types.

react.definition: React itself ships plain JS but is written with TypeScript types — most projects use .tsx with typed props, hooks and events for safety.

angular.definition: Angular is TypeScript-first — decorators, DI and templates all assume typed classes. Write Angular without TS and you lose most of its power.

next.definition: Next.js is TypeScript-first too — app router, server actions and API routes all have first-class typed APIs with generated route types.

ts.definition: TypeScript adds: interfaces & type aliases, generics, union/literal types, type narrowing, enums, decorators (Angular) and compile-time guarantees JS lacks.

react.definition: Huge ecosystem: React Native (mobile), thousands of libs, most job postings ask for it. Freedom means more decisions — router, state, styling, testing.

angular.definition: Batteries included: CLI scaffolds everything, Material UI official, RxJS integrated, strong typing throughout. Fewer choices, more consistency, steeper curve.
angular.code:
ng new my-app        // CLI generates everything
ng generate component user
ng add @angular/material

// opinionated = consistent teams, faster onboarding

next.definition: Next.js by Vercel is the default React framework for production — SSR/SSG, edge runtime, image optimisation, analytics. Backed by a company, huge adoption.

ts.definition: TypeScript is the industry's typed-JS standard — used by Angular (required), Next.js (first-class), React (de facto), Node.js backends and tooling.
